Record: Yes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Leila Nguyen (Redwood Runtime Eng), Maya Liang (Polaris Head of ML), Omar Haddad (Polaris Platform), Priya Rao (Polaris Security), Evan Brooks (Polaris NLP)
summary: Deep technical session focused on architecting Redwood runtime to support 512k token working sets on Polaris on‑prem hardware. Covered KV tiling/sharding, eviction policies, continuous batching, quantization tradeoffs for latency-sensitive workloads, and VPC/HSM constraints for on‑prem deployments. Agreed next step: run benchmark on Polaris dev cluster with representative traces.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Avery: okay everyone welcome thanks for squeezing this in, um today we wanted to dig into your 512k context goal and the on‑prem latency constraints, make sure we can meet your SLOs and outline a benchmark plan.
[00:00:12] Maya: thanks Avery, yeah we've had some internal POC tests but things blow up after about 200 to 250k, the kv cache thrashes, and latency spikes beyond our 500ms SLO for first token. so curious how Redwood handles tiled kv and what quantization options look like.
[00:00:30] Samir: quick clarifying q, when you say 500ms first token is that p50 for single‑request inference or p95 for burst traffic?
[00:00:38] Maya: p95 for single‑request interactive flows, background batch can be slower. most interactive sessions are user‑facing.
[00:00:45] Omar: also worth saying our on‑prem fleet is mixed — A100s and H100s, around 12 nodes, but network is constrained between racks, so cross‑node KV fetches add nontrivial latency.
[00:00:57] Leila: good, that helps. so primary levers are where kv lives (local GPU memory, remote shard, or persistent store), tiling/sharding strategy, and prefix/k‑v cache hit rate. we can trade off latency with memory footprint via quantization and lazy loading.
[00:01:12] Evan: can you expand on tiling? I'm used to just sharding per‑kv collection across GPUs but not sure how kernel tiling interacts.
[00:01:20] Samir: yeah so there are two orthogonal things: logical KV sharding (which key ranges live on which device) and kernel tiling/ops-level tiling — how we lay out kv blocks to optimize memory bandwidth and attention kernels. for 512k contexts, contiguous rotary or positional blocks get big, so we pack tiles to keep GPU mem accesses coalesced.
[00:01:41] Samir: shorthand: we group tokens into 'tiles' of e.g., 4k or 8k, and maintain a two‑level index so we can fetch whole tiles cheaply rather than individually pulling tiny KV rows. that reduces PCIe and NVLink chatter when fetching remote tiles.
[00:02:01] Maya: ok so that implies eviction at tile granularity, yes? we can't evict a single token.
[00:02:07] Leila: correct, eviction is coarse. we use a hybrid LRU + frequency score so hot prefixes stay resident. eviction threshold is configurable per deployment; on‑prem you can tune it aggressive if you have bandwidth to backfill from an SSD layer.
[00:02:22] Priya: security question — if tiles are stored across nodes, how do we ensure keys are encrypted and accessed only with customer KMS? HSM?
[00:02:29] Avery: good point. for Private deployments we support customer‑managed KMS; secrets never leave your VPC. remote tile transport is encrypted via mTLS and we support integrating with on‑prem HSM for key unwraps. needs a small agent on the host to do attestation for HSM calls.
[00:02:43] Priya: great. could you supply the attest/agent docs?
[00:02:45] Avery: yes we'll include in the security pack.
[00:02:47] Evan: back to perf — what's the expected per‑token cost impact of int8 quant vs int4 or more aggressive q? we need to know latency hit.
[00:02:55] Samir: generally int8/llm.int8 gives 1.7–2.2x throughput improvement on A100/H100 depending on kernel quality and sequence length. latency per token often improves, but for long context you get memory tradeoffs: quantization reduces KV tile memory so more tiles stay in cache — that usually benefits latency. int4 is trickier; many kernels are experimental and can add jitter.
[00:03:17] Leila: also note some rotary/positional compaction strategies change token indexing; we have to remap token offsets when using sparse attention. that remapping cost is CPU bound and can add tens of ms for large fetches if not optimized.
[00:03:30] Maya: we've seen jitter — sometimes 100ms extra — when switching from dense to sparse layers in our POC. is there an approach to amortize that?
[00:03:38] Samir: yes, two approaches: 1) background async rehydration of likely next tiles based on session heuristics so user requests hit warm tiles, 2) predictive prefetch using your prompt traces — we can run your traces to build a tiny predictor that preloads hot tiles. both reduce tail latency.
[00:03:55] Omar: would predictive prefetch require persistent storage of traces in Redwood? we prefer to keep traces on our S3 and only share ephemeral samples.
[00:04:03] Avery: we don't need full traces; just a sampled prefix distribution is enough. you control export; we can run offline analysis on your side or you can give us a hashed telemetry bucket.
[00:04:12] Evan: what about continuous batching? you mentioned earlier you support dynamic batching windows; how does that interact with the latency SLO?
[00:04:20] Samir: continuous batching is workload aware: we dynamically open micro‑windows (3–12ms) to aggregate concurrent requests. for interactive SLOs we use aggressive max latency caps so batching won't hold beyond your SLO. the trick at 512k is that per‑request KV fetch cost dominates, so batching mostly helps GPU throughput for the transformer compute, but not the KV fetchs if they are remote.
[00:04:40] Leila: another levers is split scheduling: do prefix/KV fetch and attention assembly while overlapping compute for newer tokens. we pipeline early to hide memory fetch latency. but this requires precise kernel scheduling and pinned memory to avoid memcpy stalls.
[00:04:55] Priya: can Redwood run inside our VPC with private networking only? we can't allow egress for model weights.
[00:05:02] Avery: yes Private deployment mode supports fully air‑gapped and VPC‑only setups. for model weights we support on‑prem hosting; control plane can be customer‑managed. we also have an on‑prem installer that doesn't phone home.
[00:05:11] Maya: is there an estimate for engineering lift? rolling your runtime vs bringing hybrid hosted?
[00:05:16] Avery: typical Private install is 6–12 weeks for full production with our dedicated support, depends on compliance checks. a hybrid Dedicated+Private ramp is faster if you start with Redwood hosted routing for non‑sensitive flows.
[00:05:26] Evan: curious about memory compaction — do you use compressed kv formats (e.g., fp16 packed or block quant) for tiles to save host memory?
[00:05:33] Samir: yes we use block quant with metadata for tile offsets. the tiles are stored compressed (fp16 or int8) and expanded on GPU as needed. compression reduces memory but requires an unpack step; again we prefer to pack to reduce remote fetch size.
[00:05:46] Omar: network layout question: if a tile is remote but on same rack via NVLink or PCIe peer‑access, it's much cheaper; cross‑rack is the killer. can Redwood prefer intra‑rack placement?
[00:05:56] Leila: absolutely. placement policy is pluggable — we prefer rack‑aware sharding so hot prefixes stay rack‑local. for on‑prem we can integrate with your cluster scheduler to enforce anti‑affinity / affinity rules.
[00:06:07] Maya: what about fallback when a tile misses and backfills from SSD — user sees a delay, can you degrade gracefully?
[00:06:13] Samir: we have a staged fallback: 1) if tile absent, try remote GPU shard (fast), 2) if remote shard misses, async fetch from local NVMe with a small priority boost, and 3) as last resort, fall back to a trimmed local context window and signal degraded quality. the app can choose to show a loading spinner or continue with a short prefix.
[00:06:28] Evan: that behavior sounds good. how do you measure quality degradation? do you run automatic evals?
[00:06:33] Leila: Redwood Optimize ties quality monitors to prompt sets; we can run evals comparing full context vs trimmed outputs on your holdout prompts and produce a delta score. we'll include thresholds for acceptable degradation.
[00:06:44] Priya: re: logging and audit — we need per‑token access logs for compliance. is that feasible without leaking content?
[00:06:50] Avery: yes we emit metadata‑only logs by default (token counts, tile ids touched, latencies). content logging can be turned on with consent and stored in your VPC. audit logs are exportable to your SIEM.
[00:06:59] Maya: practical question: what's the expected CPU overhead for large tile indexing? our CPU is limited.
[00:07:06] Samir: index remapping is CPU heavy but we use low‑latency C++ libs and SIMD for remap. typical overhead is 5–20% CPU per GPU depending on tile size and indexing complexity. if CPU is tight, we push remap64 to a small helper process on the GPU host or use hardware offload where available.
[00:07:22] Omar: can you share a recommended host sizing doc for our mixed H100/A100 cluster?
[00:07:26] Avery: yes, Samir will share host sizing with tile size recommendations.
[00:07:29] Samir: quick note on kernel selection — for longer sequences we pick attention kernels that favor memory streaming over full dense matmul; on H100 we have fused kernels that are optimized for large kv slices and reduce p95 by 15–25% in our internal tests. on A100 the window is smaller.
[00:07:44] Evan: is that something we can reproduce? we'd like to run a microbenchmark on our hardware.
[00:07:49] Samir: absolutely. we'll provide a harness that runs the fused kernel path and the fallback path so you can compare. it includes synthetic sequences up to 512k and your real traces.
[00:07:58] Maya: about quant profiles — what do you recommend for our use case which is interactive responses with long context and strong coherence needs?
[00:08:06] Leila: start with llm.int8 weight quant + fp16 activations, run quality evals with your historical prompts. if quality delta < 1–2% on your metrics, roll to production. only move to int4 if latency and cost needs force it and after thorough eval.
[00:08:21] Priya: any known failure modes to watch for on‑prem?
[00:08:24] Samir: network partitioning can cause tile thrash; ensure NVMe backplane is healthy and monitor remote fetch rates. also watch for GPU memory fragmentation when using many different model variants; pinned allocation and periodic compaction help.
[00:08:38] Maya: excellent. can we recap the benchmark plan now?
[00:08:42] Avery: yes. Plan: 1) Polaris provides 3 days of sampled prompt traces and a small holdout test set; 2) Redwood runs two benchmark suites on Polaris dev: synthetic microbench for kernel paths (dense vs fused) and full trace replay with realistic arrival patterns; 3) measure p50/p95 first token and throughput, KV hit rates, network cross‑rack fetchs, and quality deltas; 4) we iterate tile size and quant profile.
[00:09:09] Evan: timeline?
[00:09:11] Avery: aim to start perf runs the week of Dec 6, initial results by Dec 10, follow‑up meeting week of Dec 13.
[00:09:18] Maya: sounds good. any blockers?
[00:09:20] Priya: I'll need the security pack before we run anything on dev; can't allow any remote agents until attestation is set.
[00:09:28] Avery: understood; we'll send the pack and the agent attestation doc.
[00:09:31] Samir: quick note — for the dev benchmark we'll ask to bind a few cores for remap helper and reserve one GPU per node for control traffic to avoid contention.
[00:09:40] Omar: fine, we'll carve that out.
[00:09:43] Maya: thanks everyone. any last questions?
[00:09:46] Evan: just one — do you have any references of other on‑prem customers who ran 512k experiments? we can be strict on anonymization.
[00:09:53] Avery: yes we have a couple; we'll share anonymized benchmark summaries and config templates.
[00:09:58] Maya: perfect. thanks team, appreciate the depth.
[00:10:02] Avery: great, we'll send notes and the harness. meeting adjourned.
[00:10:07] ----- end of recorded segment (remaining time used for side conversations)
